<p class="lx-eyebrow">One wind and storage project, one typical year, 2025 dollars (illustrative)</p><p>150 MW of wind and a 50 MW, 4-hour battery cost $325.4M to build. A typical year's cash:</p><table class="lx-mini-table x5-led"><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Wind sales</th><td>444,132 MWh × $50/MWh</td><td class="n">$22.2M</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Battery earnings after charging</th><td>73,000 MWh discharged × $42.53/MWh margin</td><td class="n">$3.1M</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Remaining operating costs</th><td>fixed upkeep of the wind farm and the battery</td><td class="n">− $7.9M</td></tr><tr class="tot"><th scope="row">Cash available for debt service</th><td>what is left to pay the loan</td><td class="n">$17.4M</td></tr></tbody></table><p class="lx-eyebrow">The capital stack: three layers in the order they are repaid, then a grant, which is not</p><ul class="x5-fbl"><li><b>Senior debt</b><ul><li>Who: Banks and other lenders.</li><li>Gets: Fixed loan payments: interest, plus repayment of the amount borrowed (the principal).</li><li>Paid: First, right after operating costs; the project's assets pledged as security (collateral) and rules the borrower must follow (covenants) protect it, so it asks a lower return than equity.</li></ul></li><li><b>Tax equity</b><ul><li>Who: Large firms with tax bills to cut, such as banks and insurers.</li><li>Gets: Most of the tax credits (cuts to its own tax bill) and the tax deductions for the equipment's wear (depreciation), plus some cash.</li><li>Paid: After the loan and ahead of the sponsor, on terms set in advance; it carries less risk than sponsor equity.</li></ul></li><li><b>Sponsor equity</b><ul><li>Who: The developer or owner: its own money.</li><li>Gets: What is left after everyone else; often the highest return asked.</li><li>Paid: Last: the first to lose when cash falls short.</li></ul></li><li><b>Grant</b><ul><li>Who: A public program, for example DOE's program for communities of 10,000 people or fewer.</li><li>Gets: Nothing back in cash; the project meets the program's conditions.</li><li>Paid: Never: it lowers what everyone else must put in.</li></ul></li></ul><p class="lx-hint">This example assumes project-level debt, paid before either equity investor: operating costs first, then the loan, then tax equity, then the sponsor. Other deal structures order the cash differently.</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table x5-fbt"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Sold under contract</th><th scope="col">Largest loan</th><th scope="col">Share of the cost</th><th scope="col">Sponsor's share with no tax equity or grant</th><th scope="col">Bad-year coverage</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>100%</td><td>$125.7M</td><td>39%</td><td>61%</td><td>1.13</td></tr><tr><td>50%</td><td>$103.7M</td><td>32%</td><td>68%</td><td>0.96</td></tr><tr><td>0%</td><td>$81.7M</td><td>25%</td><td>75%</td><td>0.68</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="lx-hint">The toy lender sizes one loan on the contracted share of the cash, at 1.30, and one on the market share, at 2.00, then adds them; both ratios are illustrative.</p><p class="lx-hint">Loan at 6.5% over 15 years, no inflation. A bad year, illustrative: 10% less wind and market prices 40% lower.</p><p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you build the stack step by step: tap its layers, size the loan, sell less under contract, add tax equity and a grant, and see who loses first in a bad year.</p>
<!-- x05-fallback:end -->
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-datanote x5-note"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><ul>
<li><b>Illustrative.</b> Prairie Town's wind farm (fictional) with lesson A2's battery; one typical year in 2025 dollars stands for every year.</li>
<li><b>The lender.</b> Its two coverage ratios are the toy's own, within the range NREL's 2025 ATB assumes; the ATB's ratios differ by technology, not by contract.</li>
<li><b>Anchored.</b> Building costs, upkeep and output come from lessons 7 and 13 (EIA and NREL data); the contract price from lesson A1.</li>
</ul></div>
<p class="lx-hint" style="margin-top:10px">Need a refresher? <a href="a01-project-tea.html">A1</a> on cash flows and the cost of capital; <a href="a02-contracts-risk.html">A2</a> on contracts and who carries each risk.</p>

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="x05-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- x05-ideas:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>A capital stack</dt><dd>A big project's money comes in layers: senior debt, tax equity, the sponsor's own equity and sometimes a grant.</dd><dt>Order of payment</dt><dd>With project-level debt, as here, cash pays operating costs, then the loan, then tax equity, then the sponsor; the sponsor is paid last and loses first.</dd><dt>Coverage</dt><dd>A lender sizes the loan so the cash available for debt service covers each payment by a margin, the debt-service coverage ratio.</dd><dt>Why contracts matter</dt><dd>With the same expected revenue, this project supports $125.7M of debt fully contracted and $81.7M fully merchant.</dd><dt>Illustrative</dt><dd>One typical year in 2025 dollars with no inflation; the lender's coverage ratios are the toy's own; no taxes, tax-equity terms or reserve accounts.</dd></dl>
<!-- x05-ideas:end -->
</div>
</div>
<!-- x05-stop:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-card xs-stop" id="x05-stop"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Where we stop</p><h3>This side topic stops at the capital stack</h3><p class="xs-stop-lede">Finance enters the course as who puts in money, who is paid first and why lenders value contracts; structuring deals is a profession of its own.</p><div class="xs-stop-cols"><div><h4 class="xs-h">This side topic covers</h4><ul><li>The four layers of a capital stack and the order in which they are paid.</li><li>How a lender sizes a loan from cash flow and a coverage ratio.</li><li>Why contracted revenue supports more debt than revenue sold at market prices.</li></ul></div><div><h4 class="xs-h">Left to specialists</h4><ul><li>Structuring a deal: how a tax-equity partnership divides cash over time, loans to the sponsor alone, reserve accounts, term sheets.</li><li>Tax law, eligibility for credits and accounting standards.</li><li>Investment advice: this lesson rates no project and no investor.</li></ul></div></div><h4 class="xs-h">Read next, three rungs</h4><ol class="xs-ladder"><li><b>Start here.</b> Sections 4 and 6 walk through each source of capital, the debt-service coverage ratio and how financing changes a wind project's cost. <span class="xs-src"><a href="https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy17osti/68227.pdf">Schwabe, Feldman, Fields and Settle, Wind Energy Finance in the United States (NREL/TP-6A20-68227)</a>, August 2017</span></li><li><b>Go further.</b> The financing assumptions behind each technology's cost: interest rates, returns, coverage ratios and the tax-equity partnership. <span class="xs-src"><a href="https://atb.nlr.gov/electricity/2025/financial_cases_&amp;_methods">NLR, 2025 Electricity ATB, Financial Cases and Methods</a>, 2025 edition, read 7 November 2026</span></li><li><b>Go deep.</b> Build a project's cash flows with debt sizing and tax equity in a free model, with its financial documentation; then an introductory project-finance textbook. <span class="xs-src">NREL System Advisor Model (SAM), financial models documentation, free software, cited by name</span></li></ol></div>
<!-- x05-stop:end -->
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Sizing a loan, in words</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<!-- x05-deeper:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p>The lender's rule in words: the yearly loan payment may be at most the cash available for debt service divided by the coverage it asks.</p><p class="x5-eq">largest payment = <span class="lx-term" data-term="cash-flow-available-for-debt-service">CFADS</span> ÷ <span class="lx-term" data-term="debt-service-coverage-ratio">DSCR</span></p><ul><li><b>Fully contracted:</b> $17.383M ÷ 1.30 = $13.372M a year; at 6.5% over 15 years that payment repays a loan of $125.73M.</li><li><b>Fully merchant:</b> $17.383M ÷ 2.00 = $8.692M a year, which repays $81.73M.</li><li><b>In between:</b> each share of the cash carries its own loan; at 50% contracted, half of each: ($125.73M + $81.73M) ÷ 2 = $103.73M.</li><li><b>From a payment to a loan:</b> lesson <a href="a01-project-tea.html">A1</a> shows how a rate and a term turn a yearly amount into an amount today.</li></ul>
<!-- x05-deeper:end -->
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>What this example leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>One structure.</b> Project-level debt paid before both equity investors; other structures order the cash differently (NREL, 2017, pp. 15-18).</li>
<li><b>One typical year.</b> Lenders also test a loan against years of poorer output, not only a typical one (NREL, 2017, p. 18).</li>
<li><b>No taxes or inflation.</b> The toy leaves out taxes, depreciation and inflation; the 2025 ATB's financial cases include them.</li>
<li><b>Read on.</b> The three rungs of the box above go from a survey of wind finance to a free cash-flow model.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="x05-myth"><div class="lx-qq" data-id="debtcost" data-answer="myth"><p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Debt is the most expensive money in a project's capital stack.”</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Debt is paid first and protected by the project's assets pledged as security, so it asks a lower return than equity: the 2025 ATB assumes 6.5% for term debt and more for equity.</p></details></div></div><div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="x05"><div class="lx-qq" data-id="dscr" data-answer="b"><p class="lx-qtext">A project's cash available for debt service is $17.4M a year and its loan payment is $13.4M. What is its debt-service coverage ratio?</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">About 0.77</li><li data-value="b">About 1.30</li><li data-value="c">About 2.30</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$17.4M ÷ $13.4M = 1.30: the cash covers the payment 1.30 times. The ratio is cash over payment, not payment over cash (0.77).</p></details></div></div>
<!-- x05-check:end -->
